chapter.name: Exploring Substances: Acidic, Basic, and Neutral

questions.q: Litmus, which is used to test whether a substance is acidic or basic, is a natural substance obtained from
questions.a: Litmus is obtained from lichens.

questions.q: Which of these samples from the chapter's litmus activity turns red litmus paper blue?
questions.a: Washing powder solution is basic, so it turns red litmus blue. Tamarind water and amla juice are acidic and salt solution is neutral.

questions.q: In Activity 2.2, the edible samples that turned blue litmus paper red were all found to taste sour. Substances that taste sour tend to be
questions.a: Acidic. Lemon juice, amla juice, tamarind water and vinegar all taste sour, and sour-tasting substances tend to contain acids.

questions.q: Kiran's Group A (samples that turned blue litmus paper red) reads: amla juice, tamarind water, lime water, vinegar. Which sample is wrongly placed, and in which group does it belong?
questions.a: Lime water, which belongs in Group B. Lime water is a solution of calcium hydroxide, not the juice of the fruit lime; it is basic and turns red litmus blue.
o: Lime water; Group B (turns red litmus blue)
Lime water; Group C (changes neither paper)
Tamarind water; Group B (turns red litmus blue)

questions.q: Assertion (A): Bitter gourd (karela) has a bitter taste. Reason (R): Every substance that tastes bitter is basic in nature.
questions.a: A is true but R is false: bases generally taste bitter, but not everything bitter is basic; bitter gourd is bitter yet not basic.
o: A is true, but R is false.
Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.q: Read the statements. I. Amla juice and vinegar would both leave red litmus paper red. II. Tap water turns red litmus paper blue. III. Lime water is a solution of calcium hydroxide in water. Which of these are correct?
questions.a: I and III only. Amla juice and vinegar are acidic, and acids do not change red litmus. Tap water is neutral, so it changes neither litmus paper.

questions.q: (a) What is an acid-base indicator? (b) State the caution the chapter gives about tasting substances.
questions.a: (a) A substance that shows different colours in acidic and basic solutions. (b) Do not taste anything until asked to do so, and never taste an unknown substance.
s: Indicator defined as a substance showing different colours in acidic and basic solutions
Caution: do not taste anything until asked; never taste an unknown substance

questions.q: True or False: 'Salt solution is neutral, because it changes the colour of neither red nor blue litmus paper.' Give the verdict and the reason.
questions.a: True. A substance that turns neither blue litmus red nor red litmus blue is neither acidic nor basic, so it is neutral; salt solution behaves this way.
s: Verdict: True
Reason: no change in either litmus paper means neither acidic nor basic

questions.q: From the samples tested in the chapter's litmus activity, name (a) two acidic substances, (b) two basic substances and (c) one neutral substance.
questions.a: (a) Any two of lemon juice, amla juice, tamarind water, vinegar. (b) Any two of soap solution, baking soda solution, lime water, washing powder solution. (c) Any one of tap water, sugar solution, salt solution.
s: Two correct acidic substances
Two correct basic substances
One correct neutral substance

questions.q: Pooja dips a red litmus strip in liquid X and it turns blue. She then dips the same strip, now blue, in liquid Y and it turns red. She says: 'X is basic and Y is acidic.' Do you agree? Explain what each change shows.
questions.a: Yes. Red litmus turning blue shows X is basic. The strip is then blue litmus, and blue litmus turning red shows Y is acidic.
s: X basic: red litmus turned blue
The strip now acts as blue litmus, which turns red in Y, so Y is acidic
Verdict: agrees with Pooja

questions.q: The chapter's litmus activity tests eleven samples: lemon juice, soap solution, amla juice, tamarind water, vinegar, baking soda solution, lime water, tap water, washing powder solution, sugar solution and salt solution. (a) Sort them into acidic, basic and neutral groups and give the number in each group. (b) Which group changes blue litmus, and which changes red litmus? (c) Raghav has 11 blue litmus strips and 6 red litmus strips. He tests every sample on blue litmus first, and then tests only the samples that left blue litmus unchanged on red litmus. How many red strips does he need, and does he have enough? (d) If he runs short, what can he say about the sample he could not test on red litmus, and why?
questions.a: (a) Acidic 4: lemon juice, amla juice, tamarind water, vinegar. Basic 4: soap solution, baking soda solution, lime water, washing powder solution. Neutral 3: tap water, sugar solution, salt solution. (b) Acids turn blue litmus red; bases turn red litmus blue. (c) The 4 basic and 3 neutral samples leave blue litmus unchanged, so he needs 4 + 3 = 7 red strips; he has only 6, one short. (d) He only knows that it is not acidic: it could be basic or neutral, because both leave blue litmus unchanged and only red litmus can tell them apart.
s: Correct acidic and basic groups with 4 each
Correct neutral group with 3
Blue litmus changed by acids, red litmus by bases
7 red strips needed (4 basic + 3 neutral); he has 6, one short
Untested sample is not acidic but could be basic or neutral; only red litmus separates them

questions.q: Before the cooks wash the steel vessels, the Class 7 science club of a school in Madurai tests four liquids from the school canteen. A drop of lemon juice turns blue litmus paper red. A drop of tamarind water also turns blue litmus paper red. A drop of the dish-wash liquid turns red litmus paper blue, and the liquid feels slippery between the fingers. A drop of salt solution changes neither litmus paper. (a) Name the two liquids that are acidic. (b) Lemon juice and tamarind water are both edible. What taste do they share, and what does that taste suggest about a substance? (c) State the nature of the dish-wash liquid, and give one observation from the passage, other than litmus, that supports it. (d) State the nature of the salt solution, with the reason.
questions.a: (a) Lemon juice and tamarind water, because both turn blue litmus red. (b) Both taste sour; substances that taste sour tend to contain acids and are acidic. (c) Basic: it turns red litmus blue, and it feels slippery, as basic substances generally do. (d) Neutral, because it changes neither red nor blue litmus paper.
s: (a) Lemon juice and tamarind water
(b) Sour taste; sour substances tend to be acidic
(c) Basic; feels slippery (basic substances are slippery to touch)
(d) Neutral: neither litmus paper changes

questions.q: Which of these is NOT named in the chapter as something that can act as a natural acid-base indicator?
questions.a: Common salt is not named; it is a neutral substance. Beetroot, purple cabbage and jamun are named as natural indicators.

questions.q: According to the chapter, the hydrangea plant, whose flower colour depends on the nature of the soil, grows in
questions.a: Cooler climates in the Himalayan region and the North-eastern states.
o: cooler climates in the Himalayan region and the North-eastern states
the dry plains of the Deccan plateau

questions.q: While preparing red rose extract, which step should be done only under the supervision of an adult?
questions.a: Pouring hot water into the tumbler over the crushed petals.
o: Pouring hot water over the crushed petals
Placing the crushed petals in a glass tumbler

questions.q: Zoya adds red rose extract to four test tubes holding tamarind water, lime water, salt solution and vinegar. In how many tubes does the extract show a shade of red?
questions.a: 2: tamarind water and vinegar are acidic and give red. Lime water is basic and gives green; salt solution is neutral and gives no change.

questions.q: Match each step of preparing red rose extract in Column I with the detail in Column II. Column I: 1. Collect petals; 2. Crush the petals; 3. Cover the tumbler; 4. Filter. Column II: (a) using a mortar and pestle; (b) wait 5 to 10 minutes till the water becomes coloured; (c) pick fallen petals instead of plucking flowers; (d) the liquid obtained is the indicator.
questions.a: 1-c, 2-a, 3-b, 4-d: fallen petals are collected, crushed with a mortar and pestle, covered in hot water till it is coloured, and the filtrate is the extract.

questions.q: Assertion (A): Red rose extract can be used to test whether a substance is acidic, basic or neutral. Reason (R): Red rose extract gives red colour in acidic solutions, green colour in basic solutions and no change in neutral ones.
questions.a: Both are true and R explains A: because the extract shows different results in the three kinds of solution, it can sort substances like litmus does.
o: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.q: (a) Name two plants, flowers or vegetables, other than red rose, that the chapter says can act as acid-base indicators. (b) What must a substance do to be called an acid-base indicator?
questions.a: (a) Any two of beetroot, purple cabbage, turmeric, Indian blackberry (jamun) and red hibiscus (gudhal). (b) It must show different colours in acidic and basic solutions.
s: (a) Any two of beetroot, purple cabbage, turmeric, jamun, red hibiscus
(b) Shows different colours in acidic and basic solutions

questions.q: Red rose extract turns green when sample A is added and shows no change when sample B is added. (a) Name one substance from the chapter that could be A and one that could be B. (b) What will you observe if sample B is tested with red litmus paper?
questions.a: (a) A is basic, for example soap solution or lime water; B is neutral, for example sugar solution or salt solution. (b) Red litmus stays red, because a neutral substance does not change it.
s: (a) A basic example and B neutral example named correctly
(b) Red litmus stays red, as B is neutral

questions.q: Rajat adds red rose extract to three samples: (a) vinegar, (b) lime water and (c) tap water. State the colour of the extract in each.
questions.a: (a) Red, as vinegar is acidic. (b) Green, as lime water is basic. (c) No change, as tap water is neutral.
s: (a) Red with vinegar
(b) Green with lime water
(c) No change with tap water

questions.q: Sunil adds red rose extract to a clear liquid and sees no change in colour. He says: 'So the liquid must be tap water.' Is he right? Explain.
questions.a: Only partly. No change shows the liquid is neutral, so tap water is possible. But sugar solution and salt solution are also neutral and give no change, so the extract cannot tell which neutral liquid it is.
s: No change means the liquid is neutral
Other neutral liquids such as sugar or salt solution give the same result
Verdict: partly right; nature is known but the liquid cannot be named

questions.q: A Class 7 group must sort six samples (lemon juice, vinegar, soap solution, lime water, sugar solution and tap water) into acidic, basic and neutral. It has 8 blue litmus strips, only 3 red litmus strips and enough red rose extract for exactly 6 tests. (a) How many tests are needed if only red rose extract is used? (b) If each sample is first tested with blue litmus and only the unchanged ones are then tested with red litmus, how many strips of each colour are needed? (c) Sort the six samples. (d) Which plan can the group actually carry out with this stock? Show it using your counts from (a) and (b).
questions.a: (a) 6 tests, one per sample, since the extract shows red, green or no change. (b) 6 blue strips, then 4 red strips for the 4 samples that leave blue unchanged (soap solution, lime water, sugar solution, tap water). (c) Acidic: lemon juice, vinegar. Basic: soap solution, lime water. Neutral: sugar solution, tap water. (d) Only the red rose extract plan: it needs 6 tests and 6 are available. The litmus plan needs 4 red strips but there are only 3, so one sample would be left as either basic or neutral.
s: (a) 6 tests with red rose extract
(b) 6 blue and 4 red strips
(c) All six samples correctly sorted
(d) Extract plan chosen: 6 tests fit the stock, the litmus plan needs 4 red strips but only 3 exist

questions.q: In Shillong, a school science club prepares red rose extract from fallen petals and records these results. Amla juice: red. Lime water: green. Sugar solution: no change. Unknown liquid K: green. Unknown liquid M: red. (a) What is the nature of sugar solution? (b) What will liquid K do to red litmus paper? (c) Which of the five liquids would turn blue litmus paper red? (d) Litmus is running short, and the principal asks whether the club can use red rose extract instead next year. The tests will be read by Tashi, a club member who cannot tell red from green apart, though he sees blue and red as different. Decide which indicator the club should use when Tashi reads the tests, using both the data and Tashi's condition.
questions.a: (a) Neutral, as it gives no change. (b) K is basic, so it turns red litmus blue. (c) Amla juice and M, the two that gave red. (d) The data show the extract sorts the samples correctly (red for acidic, green for basic, no change for neutral, the same groups litmus gives), so in general it can replace litmus. But its acidic and basic results are red and green, which Tashi cannot tell apart, while litmus shows red against blue, which he can. So the club should keep litmus when Tashi reads the tests (or let another member read the extract).
s: (a) Sugar solution neutral
(b) K basic, turns red litmus blue
(c) Amla juice and M
(d) Extract sorts correctly by the data, but red/green results unreadable for Tashi; keep litmus (red/blue) for him

questions.q: Substances whose odours change in an acidic or a basic medium are called
questions.a: Olfactory indicators.

questions.q: A drop of baking soda solution falls on a strip of turmeric paper. The strip turns
questions.a: Red, because baking soda solution is basic and turmeric turns red in basic solutions.

questions.q: Turmeric, called a 'golden' spice in the chapter, is a member of which plant family?
questions.a: The ginger family.

questions.q: Asha tests one liquid X with three indicators and records: blue litmus paper turned red; turmeric paper turned red; red rose extract turned red. Her teacher says that one of these three records must be wrong. Which one?
questions.a: The turmeric paper record. Blue litmus turning red and red rose extract turning red both show X is acidic, and turmeric paper stays yellow in an acidic solution; it turns red only in a basic one.
o: None: all three records can be correct together

questions.q: Read the statements. I. In the onion activity, chopped onion and strips of cotton cloth are kept in a tightly closed container overnight. II. An olfactory indicator is recognised by a change in smell, not by a change in colour. III. A drop of washing powder solution and a drop of tamarind water give different colours on turmeric paper. Which of these are correct?
questions.a: I, II and III. Washing powder solution is basic and turns turmeric paper red, while tamarind water is acidic and leaves it yellow.

questions.q: Assertion (A): Turmeric paper alone can sort vinegar, soap solution and sugar solution into acidic, basic and neutral. Reason (R): Turmeric paper turns red in basic solutions.
questions.a: A is false but R is true: turmeric picks out the basic soap solution, but vinegar and sugar solution both leave it yellow, so it cannot tell acidic from neutral.
o: A is false, but R is true.
Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.

questions.q: Describe in two steps how turmeric paper is prepared.
questions.a: Make a paste of turmeric in a little water and dip a piece of filter paper in it till it turns yellow. Dry the paper and cut it into thin strips.
s: Filter paper dipped in turmeric paste till yellow
Paper dried and cut into strips

questions.q: True or False: 'Both turmeric paper and red rose extract change colour when soap solution is added to them.' Give the verdict and the reason.
questions.a: True. Soap solution is basic: turmeric paper turns red and red rose extract turns green in it.
s: Verdict: True
Reason: soap solution is basic; turmeric turns red and red rose extract turns green

questions.q: For Guru Purnima, Ashwin coats white paper with turmeric paste, dries it and writes a greeting on it with one of the tested solutions so that the words show up. (a) Of what nature must his writing solution be? (b) Name one such solution from the chapter. (c) In what colour will the words appear?
questions.a: (a) Basic, since turmeric changes colour only in basic solutions. (b) Baking soda solution (or lime water, soap solution or washing powder solution). (c) Red, on the yellow paper.
s: (a) A basic solution
(b) A correct basic solution named
(c) Red words

questions.q: In a science-club game, Tenzin is blindfolded and must find out whether each of two liquids is acidic or basic. (a) Why can litmus, red rose extract or turmeric paper not help him while he is blindfolded? (b) Which kind of indicator can he use, and which material from the chapter gives one? (c) Name one acidic liquid and one basic liquid from the chapter that he could first try on the strips to learn how each one changes the odour.
questions.a: (a) They show the result only as a change in colour, which he cannot see. (b) An olfactory indicator, whose odour changes in an acidic or basic medium: onion (strips kept with chopped onion). (c) For example tamarind water (acidic) and baking soda solution (basic), the two the chapter puts on the onion strips.
s: (a) These indicators show only a colour change, which he cannot see
(b) Olfactory indicator: onion
(c) One acidic (e.g. tamarind water) and one basic (e.g. baking soda solution) liquid

questions.q: Answer these about turmeric as an indicator. (a) What is turmeric paper made from? (b) What colour does it turn in a basic solution? (c) What colour does it show in acidic and neutral solutions? (d) A curry stain on a white shirt changes colour when soap is applied. Why? (e) State one limitation of turmeric paper as an indicator.
questions.a: (a) Filter paper dipped in turmeric paste and dried. (b) Red. (c) It stays yellow. (d) The curry contains turmeric and soap is basic, so the turmeric turns red. (e) It cannot tell an acidic substance from a neutral one.
s: (a) Filter paper with turmeric paste, dried
(b) Red in basic
(c) Stays yellow in acidic and neutral
(d) Soap is basic and turns the turmeric in curry red
(e) Cannot tell acidic from neutral

questions.q: A kirana shop owner in Nagpur wants to know the nature of three cleaning liquids before stocking them. His nephew tests them. Liquid A turns turmeric paper red. Liquid B leaves turmeric paper yellow but turns blue litmus red. Liquid C leaves turmeric paper yellow and leaves blue litmus blue. (a) What is the nature of A? (b) What is the nature of B? (c) What is the nature of C? Explain. (d) For future checks he only needs to know whether a cleaning liquid is basic, and can buy just one kind of strip: turmeric paper or blue litmus. Which should he buy? Justify.
questions.a: (a) Basic, as it turns turmeric red. (b) Acidic, as it turns blue litmus red. (c) Neutral: yellow turmeric shows it is not basic and unchanged blue litmus shows it is not acidic. (d) Turmeric paper: it turns red only in a basic liquid, while blue litmus does not change in either a basic or a neutral liquid, so it cannot show that a liquid is basic.
s: (a) A basic
(b) B acidic
(c) C neutral, using both results
(d) Turmeric paper chosen; blue litmus stays blue in both basic and neutral liquids

questions.q: Who is known as the 'Father of Modern Indian Chemistry'?
questions.a: Acharya Prafulla Chandra Ray (P.C. Ray).

questions.q: In Activity 2.7, one drop of lemon juice is mixed with about twenty drops of water, and a drop of blue litmus solution is added. The solution turns
questions.a: Red, because the diluted lemon juice is still acidic and acids turn blue litmus red.

questions.q: When an acid reacts with a base in a neutralisation reaction, what is formed?
questions.a: Salt and water, with the release of heat.
o: Salt and water, with heat released
Only salt, with heat taken in
Salt and water, with heat taken in

questions.q: In Activity 2.7, Rahul adds drops of lime water to lemon juice solution containing blue litmus solution but does not swirl the test tube. A blue streak appears where each drop falls, while the rest of the solution stays red. Why does the activity tell him to swirl the tube well after adding the drops?
questions.a: Swirling mixes the lime water through the whole solution, so the base meets all of the acid and the colour shows the nature of the whole mixture, not just of the spot where the drop fell.
o: To mix the lime water through the whole solution so that the colour shows the nature of the whole mixture
To warm the solution, because litmus changes colour only when it is warm
To make the lime water acidic before it reaches the lemon juice
To remove the salt that forms, so that the colour can change

questions.q: Assertion (A): In Activity 2.7, the colour of the lemon juice solution with blue litmus changes from red to blue as lime water is added drop by drop. Reason (R): Lime water is a base, and it neutralises the acid in the lemon juice.
questions.a: Both are true and R explains A: once enough lime water (a base) has neutralised the acid, the solution is no longer acidic, so the litmus turns from red to blue.
o: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.q: Match Column I with Column II. Column I: 1. Neutralisation; 2. Salt; 3. Heat; 4. Lime water in Activity 2.7. Column II: (a) the base added drop by drop to lemon juice; (b) the reaction between an acid and a base; (c) released during neutralisation; (d) formed along with water in neutralisation.
questions.a: 1-b, 2-d, 3-c, 4-a: neutralisation is the acid-base reaction, salt forms with water, heat is released, and lime water is the base added in Activity 2.7.

questions.q: (a) What is a neutralisation reaction? (b) Write its word equation.
questions.a: (a) The reaction between an acid and a base, mixed in sufficient quantity, that gives a solution which is neither acidic nor basic. (b) Acid + Base -> Salt + Water + Heat.
s: (a) Acid and base react to give a solution neither acidic nor basic
(b) Acid + Base -> Salt + Water + Heat

questions.q: True or False: 'In Activity 2.7, lime water neutralises the lemon juice only because blue litmus solution has been added to the test tube.' Give the verdict and the reason.
questions.a: False. Neutralisation is the reaction between the acid (lemon juice) and the base (lime water); the blue litmus solution is only an indicator that shows the change of colour from red to blue.
s: Verdict: False
Reason: the acid and base neutralise each other; litmus only indicates the change

questions.q: Give three contributions of Acharya P.C. Ray described in the chapter.
questions.a: Any three: he advanced scientific research in India; he established India's first pharmaceutical company in 1901; he wrote on the history of chemistry in India, highlighting ancient Indian scientists; he advocated the mother tongue as the medium of instruction.
s: First correct contribution
Second correct contribution
Third correct contribution

questions.q: After mixing an acid with a base, Isha puts one drop of the mixture on turmeric paper and one drop on blue litmus paper. Neither paper changes colour. She says: 'The mixture is now neutral.' Do you agree? Explain using both results.
questions.a: Yes. Turmeric paper staying yellow shows the mixture is not basic. Blue litmus staying blue shows it is not acidic. Neither acidic nor basic means neutral, so neutralisation is complete.
s: Turmeric unchanged: not basic
Blue litmus unchanged: not acidic
Verdict: agrees, the mixture is neutral

questions.q: A science club plans three demonstrations of neutralisation. Demo 1: vinegar with a drop of blue litmus solution, then lemon juice added drop by drop. Demo 2: soap solution with a drop of red litmus solution, then lime water added drop by drop. Demo 3: tamarind water with a drop of blue litmus solution, then baking soda solution added drop by drop. For each demo predict the colour seen, decide whether it shows neutralisation, and justify. Name the products of the reaction in the demo that works.
questions.a: Demo 1: red throughout; two acids, no neutralisation. Demo 2: blue throughout; two bases, no neutralisation. Demo 3: red at first, turning blue once enough baking soda solution is added; an acid and a base, so it shows neutralisation. Products: salt and water, with heat released.
s: Demo 1 stays red: both acidic, not neutralisation
Demo 2 stays blue: both basic, not neutralisation
Demo 3 red then blue
Demo 3 chosen: acid with base
Products salt and water with heat

questions.q: A Class 7 group in Bhopal puts red rose extract into vinegar and then adds baking soda solution drop by drop, noting the colour after every 5 drops. 0 drops: red. 5 drops: red. 10 drops: red. 15 drops: the same colour as the plain extract (no change). 20 drops: green. (a) What is the nature of the mixture after 5 drops? Give the reason. (b) At which reading was the mixture first seen to be neutral? (c) What does the green colour after 20 drops show? (d) Riya says: 'We should always add 20 drops, to be sure that all the acid is gone.' Decide, using the table, whether she is right.
questions.a: (a) Acidic, because the extract is still red. (b) At the 15-drop reading: the extract shows no change, so the mixture is neither acidic nor basic (it may have become neutral somewhere between 10 and 15 drops). (c) Too much baking soda solution (a base) has been added, so the mixture has become basic. (d) She is wrong: at 15 drops the acid was already neutralised, and 20 drops overshoots and makes the mixture basic, not neutral.
s: (a) Acidic, extract still red
(b) First seen neutral at the 15-drop reading (no change)
(c) Excess base: mixture basic
(d) Riya wrong: 15 drops already neutral; 20 drops makes it basic

questions.q: When a red ant bites, the acidic liquid it injects into the skin is
questions.a: Formic acid.

questions.q: For a red ant bite, soil made acidic by fertilisers and acidic factory waste, the chapter suggests moist baking soda, lime and basic substances. What do these three remedies have in common?
questions.a: Each adds a base to neutralise an acid.
o: Each adds a base to neutralise an acid
Each adds an acid to neutralise a base
Each only dilutes the problem with water

questions.q: After a red ant bite, Keerthi's brother first rubs moist sugar on the bite and the stinging goes on. He then rubs moist baking soda and the pain eases. Which explains the difference?
questions.a: Sugar is neutral, so it cannot neutralise the formic acid; baking soda is a base, so it neutralises the acid.
o: Sugar is neutral and cannot neutralise the acid, but baking soda is a base and can
Sugar is acidic and adds to the acid, but baking soda is neutral
Baking soda is acidic and dissolves the ant's acid
Sugar was rubbed before the acid had spread

questions.q: Waste water from a factory near a village pond turns blue litmus paper red, and the number of fish in the pond keeps falling. What does the chapter suggest the factory should do?
questions.a: Neutralise the acidic waste by adding basic substances to it before releasing it into the pond.
o: Add basic substances to the waste before releasing it
Add vinegar to the waste before releasing it
Release the waste directly but at night
Add sugar to the pond to feed the fish

questions.q: Read the statements. I. The fish population of a lake can decline when factory waste is released into it. II. Moist baking soda relieves a red ant bite because it is a base that neutralises the acid. III. A red ant injects a basic liquid into the skin. Which of these is/are correct?
questions.a: I and II only. The ant injects formic acid, which is acidic, not basic.

questions.q: Match each problem in Column I with its remedy in Column II. Column I: 1. Red ant bite; 2. Soil made acidic by chemical fertilisers; 3. Basic soil; 4. Acidic factory waste. Column II: (a) lime; (b) manure and composted leaves; (c) moist baking soda; (d) basic substances added before release.
True or False: 'Manure and composted leaves are added to a basic soil because they release more bases into it.' Give the verdict and the reason.
questions.a: False. Organic matter such as manure and composted leaves releases acids, and these acids neutralise the basic nature of the soil.
s: Verdict: False
Reason: organic matter releases acids that neutralise the basic soil

questions.q: Two neighbouring fields both grow poor crops. Soil water from field X turns blue litmus paper red. Soil water from field Y changes neither litmus paper. (a) For which field can neutralisation help, and why? (b) Give a likely reason for the poor crop in the other field.
questions.a: (a) Field X: its soil is acidic, and an acidic soil can be neutralised by a base. (b) Field Y's soil is neutral, so neutralisation cannot help; the poor health may be due to a deficiency of nutrients in the soil.
s: (a) Field X, as its soil is acidic and can be neutralised
(b) Field Y is neutral; likely a deficiency of nutrients

questions.q: A farmer adds lime to one half of his field and manure to the other half. Next season, soil water from the lime half leaves both litmus papers unchanged and the plants are healthy. Soil water from the manure half turns blue litmus red and the plants are weak. What was the nature of the soil before treatment? Explain using both halves.
questions.a: Acidic. Lime is a base, so it neutralised the acidic soil and that half became neutral. Manure releases acids, so it could not correct acidic soil and that half stayed acidic, turning blue litmus red.
s: Soil was acidic at the start
Lime (a base) neutralised it, so the lime half became neutral
Manure releases acids, so the manure half stayed acidic

questions.q: Gurbir lives near an industrial area. He tells Ashwin that the fish in his neighbourhood lake are declining day by day. A drop of the waste water from a nearby factory turns blue litmus paper red. (a) Give one possible cause of the fall in fish. (b) What is the nature of the waste? (c) What colour would red rose extract show with this waste? (d) The factory later treats its waste so that it is neutral before release. What would a drop of the treated waste now do to blue litmus paper?
questions.a: (a) Factory waste being released into the lake. (b) Acidic. (c) Red. (d) Nothing: blue litmus paper stays blue, because a neutral liquid does not change it.
s: (a) Factory waste released into the lake
(b) Acidic
(c) Red
(d) Blue litmus stays blue (neutral waste)

questions.q: A panchayat checks the waste water of three small factories that drain into its lake. Waste A turns blue litmus paper red. Waste B turns turmeric paper red. Waste C leaves blue litmus blue and turmeric paper yellow. (a) State the nature of each waste, with the reason. (b) Which waste should be treated by adding basic substances before release, and why? (c) The panchayat says: 'Waste C needs the same treatment as waste A.' Analyse this claim.
questions.a: (a) A acidic: blue litmus turned red. B basic: turmeric turned red. C neutral: not acidic (blue litmus unchanged) and not basic (turmeric unchanged). (b) Waste A, because acidic waste can be neutralised by adding basic substances before it is released. (c) The claim is wrong: C is already neutral, so there is no acid in it to neutralise.
s: A acidic with reason
B basic with reason
C neutral using both tests
Waste A to be treated with basic substances before release
Claim rejected: C is neutral, nothing to neutralise

questions.q: A farmer in Punjab writes on the Farmer's Portal that his wheat is growing poorly. Over three seasons he used 50 kg, 100 kg and 200 kg of chemical fertiliser per acre, and his yield fell from 20 to 16 to 11 quintals per acre. His soil water now turns blue litmus paper red. (a) By how many quintals per acre did the yield fall from the first season to the third? (b) What is the nature of his soil now? (c) Using the chapter, explain how his fertiliser use led to this. (d) He plans to use 400 kg per acre next season to push the yield back up. Decide whether this plan is sensible, using the data, and say what he should do instead.
questions.a: (a) 20 - 11 = 9 quintals per acre. (b) Acidic. (c) Excessive use of chemical fertilisers made the soil acidic, and plants do not grow well in soil that is too acidic. (d) Not sensible: every time the fertiliser went up (50, 100, 200 kg) the yield went down (20, 16, 11), because the extra fertiliser made the soil acidic; 400 kg would make it worse. He should cut the excess fertiliser and treat the soil with lime, a base that neutralises it.
s: (a) 9 quintals per acre
(b) Acidic soil
(c) Excess fertiliser made the soil acidic; plants grow poorly in too-acidic soil
(d) Plan rejected using the rising-fertiliser, falling-yield data; cut excess fertiliser and add lime
